newsitem.title: SPAIN: For Clinton, NATO debate just starting.
newsitem.headline: For Clinton, NATO debate just starting.

text.p: For U.S. President Bill Clinton, the debate over expanding the NATO alliance is only beginning.
Now that NATO is inviting three new nations to join, Clinton turns to the task of selling the idea back home.

Clinton has been advocating extending membership to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- but the idea has generated only moderate support in the United States, and some well- organised opposition.
Having convinced European leaders that only three nations should be admitted rather than five, Clinton now begins a sales pitch to convince Americans that even three invitees is not too many.

"I hope this week and the publicity it has received back home in America will help to stimulate discussion and debate among the American people about this historic decision," Clinton candidly observed as the summit concluded on Wednesday.
"And I hope that when the American people hear the arguments, they too will strongly support the enlargement of NATO," Clinton said.

It is no accident that when the U.S. president leaves Spain on Thursday, his first stop is in Poland. Polish-Americans have long been a potent political bloc in the United States, one Clinton hopes to activate for next year's debate over expansion in the Senate, the upper house of Congress.
"This is going to make all of us stronger and more secure," Clinton said, stressing what will be a central theme of his message to rally support.

Admitting that enlargement "will not be cost or risk free", Clinton stressed: "For the American people, clearly the cost will be far less in lives and money to expand the bounds of democracy and security than it would be if we had to involve our people in another conflict in Europe."
The "cost" and "risk" of agreeing to a NATO expansion are two of the key issues being raised by opponents of enlarging the alliance.

As the White House and Congress haggle over ways to reduce the U.S. budget deficit, with intense arguments over what programmes should be spared and which ones ought to be cut back, critics claim the added costs of a larger NATO only make matters worse.
Clinton contends that the cost of expansion to the United States would only be $200 million a year for the next decade -- a mere trifle out of an annual budget of more than $1 trillion.

Opponents, mindful that voters are sensitive about anything that hits their wallets, counter that the added costs of integrating the three new members into the alliance will be offset by unpopular cuts in programmes already facing fiscal restraints.
They also point out that some NATO allies believe Washington has underestimated the cost of enlargement and that some cost projections are significantly higher than Clinton's.

The "risk" argument of expansion critics boils down to the military obligation that comes with NATO membership. If approved by the U.S. Senate, the enlargement commits the United States to send its troops to protect the three former Warsaw Pact nations from any outside threat.
Clinton contends the risk would be far greater for the United States if it did not invest in creating a Europe "undivided, free and at peace".
U.S. officials say they have been mapping out a long-range strategy for generating support for the expansion -- expecting a vote on ratification in the Senate would come next June.
Clinton -- along with White House, State Department and Defence Department officials -- plans a series of appearances to promote the NATO changes.
"The president is going to be actively involved over a period of time," said Jim Steinberg, deputy director of the National Security Council.
"We will be talking to the American people about what was accomplished here and why it was important."
